Mars' Hill
marz hil
proper noun (the Areopagus at Athens)
The English rendering of the Areopagus (Greek Areios Pagos, “hill of Ares/Mars”), the council-hill of Athens where Paul preached to the philosophers (Acts 17).

📖 Biblical Definition

Mars' Hill is the Authorized Version's name for the Areopagus, the council-hill of Athens, where the apostle Paul, his spirit stirred by a city wholly given to idolatry, preached the living God to the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers. Standing in the midst of Mars' hill, Paul took the Athenians' own altar “TO THE UNKNOWN GOD” as his text and declared the God they ignorantly worshipped: the God who made the world and all things, who dwelleth not in temples made with hands, who giveth life and breath to all, and who now commandeth all men everywhere to repent, having appointed a day in which He will judge the world by the Man whom He raised from the dead. When they heard of the resurrection, some mocked, some delayed, but certain believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris. The dictionary marks Mars' Hill as the great pattern of apostolic engagement with pagan thought. Paul neither flattered the philosophers nor borrowed their authority; he quoted their poets only to turn their own words against their idolatry, and pressed home creation, providence, repentance, resurrection, and judgment. The dictionary holds it against two errors: the accommodation that would soften the gospel to please the cultured despisers, and the withdrawal that would refuse to reason with them at all. Paul did neither—he proclaimed the whole counsel of God to the wise of this world, and God called His own out of Athens by the foolishness of preaching.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Areopagus at Athens where Paul preached the living God to the philosophers (Acts 17:22-34); the pattern of apostolic engagement with pagan thought—neither flattering nor withdrawing, but proclaiming creation, repentance, resurrection, and judgment.

MARS' HILL, proper noun. [The Areopagus, “hill of Ares/Mars.”] The council-hill of Athens.

Paul preached there to the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers (Acts 17:22).

He took the altar “TO THE UNKNOWN GOD” as his text (Acts 17:23).

He declared the Creator, providence, repentance, resurrection, and judgment.

Some mocked; certain believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite (Acts 17:34).

📖 Key Scripture

Ac 17:22 — "Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious."

Ac 17:23 — "For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you."

Ac 17:30 — "And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent:"

Ac 17:34 — "Howbeit certain men clave unto him, and believed: among the which was Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the errors are the accommodation that softens the gospel to please cultured despisers, and the withdrawal that refuses to reason with the world at all.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faithful apostolic engagement with the thought of the age. One corruption reads Paul at Athens as a model of accommodation—trimming the offensive parts, borrowing the philosophers' authority, blending the gospel with the culture's wisdom to win a hearing. But Paul did the opposite: he quoted a pagan poet only to turn the words against idolatry, and pressed home creation, repentance, resurrection, and a fixed day of judgment—the very points his hearers found most foolish. He won some not by softening the message but by proclaiming it.

The opposite corruption is withdrawal—the refusal to reason with the world at all, treating every engagement with pagan thought as compromise. Paul disputed daily in the market and reasoned on Mars' hill; he met the philosophers on their ground and answered them with the truth. The dictionary holds the balance the apostle struck: neither the accommodation that empties the cross of its offence, nor the retreat that hides the light under a bushel, but the bold, reasoned proclamation of the whole counsel of God to the wise of this world—trusting God to call His own out of Athens by the foolishness of preaching.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Areopagus (Greek Areios Pagos, “hill of Ares,” the war-god the Romans called Mars), the ancient council-seat of Athens; rendered “Mars' hill” in the Authorized Version.

expand to see more

Areios Pagos, Greek, “hill of Ares,” the Athenian council-hill.

Ares, the Greek war-god, called Mars by the Romans, whence “Mars' hill.”

The seat of the Athenian council that judged matters of religion and morals.

The Epicureans and Stoics, the philosophers Paul addressed there.

The scene of Acts 17:22-34, Paul's sermon to the Athenians.

Usage

"The pastor preached Mars' hill as the pattern of engaging the wise of this world without flattering them."

"He noted Paul quoted a pagan poet only to turn the words against idolatry."

"She saw that Paul won some not by softening the resurrection but by proclaiming it."
